candidates.passage: The area of VAM-VAE, which is our backward integration project, is something which we are looking forward to strongly. candidates.passage: Vivek Maheshwari: And the second question is on volume growth. This quarter and the last, you have been doing well for the last two quarters. Part of this is essentially the base. But what do you think about the intrinsic demand in the sector? What is your outlook? And woul d love to know your thoughts on the competition. Two parts. One is the outlook on volume growth beyond the base. And the second is, the competition bit. [...] Amit Syngle: What we see is that, as I mentioned, the demand has been good both from the point of view of the rural demand as well as from the point of view of the urban centres. We expect at least some part of this demand to sustain in the market. And we have been seeing some early shoots in the months of April and May. And we basically believe that going forward, we are still looking atleast a high single -digit volume growth in terms of what we would kind of achieve.
candidates.speaker: Amit Syngle
candidates.adjudication_note: 'Going forward' has no firm date; included due management volume outlook in FY27 call context.

candidates.passage: But in quarter one, we would expect that the pipeline stocks to go up to some extent as and when a price increase is announced.
candidates.speaker: Amit Syngle
candidates.adjudication_note: No numeric magnitude; 'go up to some extent' treated as binary inventory increase; verify Gate 1.

candidates.passage: Mihir Shah: And secondly, post 2Q, you will be having a higher base, unlike a favourable base that we had seen over the past few quarters. [...] Amit Syngle: So, while there could be a little bit of upstocking, which could happen because of the price increases, we are still confident that demand conditions should continue giving us closer to high single-digit volume growth in the band of about 8 -10%, as we predict going forward.
candidates.speaker: Amit Syngle
candidates.adjudication_note: Timeframe comes from analyst question; management supplied the 8-10% band.

candidates.passage: The third area, as you rightly mentioned, is backward integration. candidates.speaker: Amit Syngle
candidates.adjudication_note: Vague 'a part of it is coming in H1' and benefits not quantified; may duplicate VAM-VAE commissioning guidance.

candidates.adjudication_note: Figure originated in analyst question; management confirmed larger impact in Q1 and Q2, but price hike itself was already taken/announced.

candidates.passage: Percy Panthaki: Hi, sir. Thanks for taking my question, I just wanted to understand this. When you are saying that you will maintain the margin guidance of 18-20%. Does this in the backend imply an assumption that the macroeconomic situation or the geopolitical situation will get resolved and the commodity prices will come down pretty quickly? Or would you say that even if crude remains in that $90 to $100 band for the rest of the year, even in that scenario, the margin guidance would remain intact? [...] Amit Syngle: As we see it, in these conditions, it is very difficult to really predict for over three to four quarters. Clearly, if we were to look at the next two quarters as something which we are seeing, the inflation levels are not going to come down so easily. It depends on where the whole war situation goes and how it really fructifies, what further impact on raw material prices it really caters. In the given scenario, we need to work very diligently, looking at maintaining our margin band.
candidates.speaker: Amit Syngle
candidates.adjudication_note: Analyst supplied 18-20%; management referred to maintaining 'margin band' for next two quarters but with qualifications; verify strength of acceptance.

candidates.passage: Percy Panthaki: Understood. The context of my question was, if I look at the last crude cycle which was FY22, at that time, also, on a Y-o-Y basis for the full year, there was about a 14% average price increase. At that time, we had finished the full year at a margin of 16.5%, FY22 consolidated. If I compare it to  FY20, because FY21 was exceptional because of cost savings, etc., FY20 was about 20.5%. There was about a 400 bps contraction in FY22 despite fairly high price increases. What is different this time which gives you the confidence to say that we have closed this year at 18.8%, you are saying the contraction would not be more than  about a 100 bps? [...] Amit Syngle: See, first of all, the current context is that,  we are looking at the first six months at this stage because it is very difficult to really predict for the full year. And as I see it, for the first six months, possibly yes, we are still open to more price increases we need to take from the current levels where we are, and that would really compensate for some deficit what we are seeing.
candidates.speaker: Amit Syngle
candidates.adjudication_note: Analyst-originated <=100 bps contraction; management answered 'for the first six months, possibly yes' and refused full-year prediction.
